River Chebar
KEE-bar
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Kebar, a river or canal in Babylonia where Ezekiel, among the exiles, received his visions of God.

Biblical Definition

The Chebar was a great river or canal in the land of the Chaldeans, by which the prophet Ezekiel dwelt among the Jewish exiles, and where he received his overwhelming visions of God. "Now it came to pass... as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God" (Ezek 1:1). There, far from the temple and the holy land, by the waters of a foreign and pagan country, the glory of the LORD appeared to Ezekiel in the vision of the four living creatures, the wheels, and the throne-chariot, with One above it in the appearance of a man surrounded with the brightness of the rainbow — "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (Ezek 1:28). By the Chebar Ezekiel was called and commissioned as a watchman to the house of Israel. The vision taught the captives a truth they sorely needed: that the glory of God was not confined to Jerusalem, but had come to His people even in Babylon, and that the sovereign LORD reigned on His throne over all the earth. The Chebar stands in the dictionary as the river of Ezekiel's visions, where God met His exiled people in a strange land, and proved that no captivity can shut His glory out, nor any distance separate His own from the presence of their God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A river or canal in Babylonia (Ezek 1:1-3) where Ezekiel, among the exiles, saw his visions of God's throne-chariot and glory; proof that God's presence was not confined to Jerusalem but came to His people even in captivity.

RIVER CHEBAR, proper noun. A river or canal in the land of the Chaldeans (Babylonia).

Where Ezekiel dwelt among the Jewish exiles.

Where the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God (Ezek 1:1).

Where he beheld the living creatures, the wheels, and the throne-chariot.

Where he was called and commissioned as a watchman to Israel.

Key Scripture

Ezek 1:1 — "Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God."

Ezek 1:3 — "The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the hand of the LORD was there upon him."

Ezek 1:28 — "...This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake."

Psa 137:1 — "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."

Modern Corruption

Chebar needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God's presence and glory reach His people even in exile, and that no captivity can confine the reign of the sovereign LORD.

expand to see more

God-confined correction. The exiles might have supposed that God's glory was bound to the temple in Jerusalem, and that in Babylon they were cut off from Him. By the Chebar God shattered that despair, bringing the vision of His throne-chariot — mobile, sovereign, unconfined — to His captive people. The dictionary holds that the LORD is not localized or limited; His glory met the exiles by a pagan river, and He is present with His people wherever they are scattered, for the whole earth is full of His glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the powers of the world. The throne-chariot vision revealed the LORD reigning above the wheels and the living creatures, governing all things even from the midst of Babylon. The dictionary commends the comfort to a scattered and pressured church: though God's people sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep (Psa 137:1), their God reigns over Babylon itself, and His glory has not abandoned them.
